title: Stock Trauma Finally Does The Trick
summary:
Stock Trauma Finally Does The Trick 

             
             
            Ever since the NASDAQ bounced off multi-month lows on November 6th, that's been the line in the sand for bonds to reconnect with the flight to safety narrative. Bond market reluctance drastically increased after last week's higher inflation readings, and that made for diminishing returns on this week's stock market slide. Bonds are still not back to those Nov 6th levels, but they were willing to take a much bigger step in that direction today after the NASDAQ blew right past its Nov 6th lows. Multiple major tech names were down over 10%, adding to a much larger slump on the week. 10yr yields were down roughly 12bps by 3pm and MBS added half a point.

title: Mortgage Rates Much Lower on Friday
summary: Mortgage rates had been making cautious improvements throughout the week with help from weakness in the stock market. Stocks have generally been providing guidance for rates since mid-October, but bonds (which dictate rates) became more and more reluctant to keep pace with the move after last week's inflation data.  It was always going to be the case that stocks would need to have a bad enough day to really catch the bond market's attention. With multiple large tech stocks down more than 10%, today certainly deserves consideration for the "bad enough" designation.   10yr Treasury yields fell more than 0.13% by 3pm ET and average 30yr fixed mortgage rates weren't far behind. After multiple lenders made mid-day adjustments, our rate index fell to 7.33% (down 0.12% from yesterday). This is the lowest level since November 10th.  [thirtyyearmortgagerates]

title: Construction Activity Still Above Pre-Pandemic Levels
summary: Residential construction delivered a mixed report in October, with housing starts and completions rebounding while building permits suffered a sizable decline. The biggest concern was single-family permitting, which fell nearly 9% from September, suggesting a weaker pipeline for future construction.  Privately owned housing starts increased  9.9%  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  1.309 million , putting them 2.8% above October 2025 levels. Single-family starts rose  4.0%  to  864k , multi-family came in at 433k.  Building permits moved in the opposite direction, falling  7.4%  to an annual rate of  1.295 million . That was also  8.7%  below year-ago levels. Single-family authorizations dropped  8.7%  to  772k , while permits for buildings with five or more units came in at 475k.    The divergence between starts and permits is worth watching. Builders began more projects in October, but the decline in authorizations points to less momentum in the pipeline, particularly for single-family construction.  Completions also rebounded, increasing  6.5%  to an annual rate of  1.272 million . However, that was still  10.4%  below October 2025 levels. Single-family completions rose  6.3%  to  900k , while multi-family completions came in at 362k.

title: Mortgage Applications Dip 2.3 Percent as Rates Bounced Back
summary:
Mortgage applications reversed course as mortgage rates moved higher for a second consecutive week. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  2.3% decline  in total application volume for the week ending November 13, 2026.  Purchase applications led the decline, falling 3% on a seasonally adjusted basis, while refinance applications decreased 2%. On an unadjusted basis, purchase activity was down 7% for the week.      Compared to year-ago levels, purchase applications remained  18% lower , while refinance activity was down  54% . The refinance share of total applications increased to 41.1% from 39.8%, while adjustable-rate mortgage applications accounted for 10.8% of activity.  MBA's Joel Kan attributed the pullback to rising rates. The average 30-year fixed rate in MBA's survey climbed to  7.35% , its highest level in three weeks. Kan also noted that FHA refinance applications increased nearly 7% despite the overall decline in refinance activity, helped by FHA rates running roughly 30 basis points below conforming rates. title: Pending Home Sales Hit Another Record Low
summary:
Pending home sales are still testing their lowest levels as contract signings weakened across the country. The National Association of REALTORS® (NAR) Pending Home Sales Index (PHSI), which tracks signed contracts on existing homes, dropped  4.7%  from September and  16.7%  from a year earlier.    October marks the second consecutive month of record-low pending sales. NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun suggested  “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,”   Still, the near-term outlook isn't encouraging. Yun warned that two consecutive months of record-low contract signings point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, adding "...annual existing-home sales could end up at their lowest level since the mid-1990s, despite the U.S. population having grown by roughly 75 million since then." title: Affordability Drives Builder Confidence to 14-Year Lows
summary:
Builder confidence fell to its lowest level in more than 14 years in November, as high mortgage rates, rising construction costs, labor shortages, and hesitant buyers continued to weigh on the housing market. The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) dropped four points to  25 , its lowest reading since April 2012. title: FHA's Capital Cushion Falls to 2.65% Under Severe Stress Test
summary: The FHA's mortgage insurance fund has more than five times the capital required by law. But under the agency's most severe economic stress test, much of that cushion disappears.FHA's Mutual Mortgage Insurance (MMI) Fund ended fiscal year 2026 with a capital ratio of 10.29%, comfortably above the 2% statutory minimum. Under a scenario modeled on the housing crisis, with adjustments that eliminate much of the subsequent recovery in home prices, the ratio falls to 2.65%.That leaves just 65 basis points above the minimum, a considerably narrower margin than the headline figure suggests.
